paragraphs: In America a woman’s independence is lost for good in the bonds of marriage. An unmarried woman is less restrained there than elsewhere, but a wife is held to stricter obligations. The one makes her father’s house a place of freedom and pleasure; the other lives in her husband’s home as if in a cloister. Yet these two conditions of life are perhaps not as opposed as one might suppose, and it is natural for American women to pass through the one to reach the other.

Religious peoples and trading nations take marriage with particular seriousness. The former consider the regularity of a woman’s life the best pledge and surest sign of the purity of her morals; the latter see it as the strongest guarantee of order and prosperity in the household. The Americans are at once a puritanical people and a commercial nation. Their religious opinions and their trading habits therefore both lead them to demand much self-denial from woman, and a constant sacrifice of her pleasures to her duties that is seldom required of her in Europe. So in the United States public opinion, which allows no exceptions, carefully confines woman within the narrow circle of domestic interests and duties and forbids her to step outside it.

When a young American woman enters the world, she finds these ideas firmly established. She sees the rules that follow from them, and she quickly realizes that she cannot depart for a moment from the established usages of her contemporaries without risking her peace of mind, her honor, even her social existence. She finds the energy for such an act of submission in the firmness of her understanding and in the manly habits her education has given her. It may be said that by using her independence she has learned to give it up, without a struggle and without a murmur, when the time comes for the sacrifice. But no American woman falls into the toils of marriage as into a snare laid for her simplicity and ignorance. She has been taught beforehand what is expected of her, and she enters this engagement voluntarily and freely. She bears her new condition with courage, because she chose it. In America paternal discipline is very relaxed and the marriage tie very strict, so a young woman does not take on the latter without considerable caution and apprehension. Early marriages are rare. American women therefore do not marry until their understandings have been exercised and have matured, whereas in other countries most women generally begin to exercise and mature their understandings only after marriage.

I do not at all suppose, however, that the great change in all the habits of women in the United States as soon as they marry should be attributed only to the pressure of public opinion. Often they impose it on themselves, by their own will alone. When the time comes to choose a husband, the cold and stern power of reasoning, educated and strengthened by free observation of the world, teaches an American woman that a spirit of levity and independence within the bonds of marriage is a constant source of annoyance, not of pleasure. It tells her that a girl’s amusements cannot become a wife’s recreations, and that the sources of a married woman’s happiness lie in her husband’s home. She sees clearly beforehand the only road that can lead to domestic happiness, so she enters upon it at once and follows it to the end without trying to turn back.

The same strength of purpose that young wives in America show in bending themselves at once, and without complaint, to the austere duties of their new condition is just as plain in all the great trials of their lives. In no country in the world are private fortunes more precarious than in the United States. It is not unusual for the same man, in the course of his life, to rise and fall again through all the grades that lead from wealth to poverty. American women endure these changes of fortune with calm and unquenchable energy. It seems that their desires shrink as easily as they grow with their fortunes. *a

Most of the adventurers who migrate every year to settle the western wilds belong, as I noted in the earlier part of this work, to the old Anglo-American race of the Northern States. Many of these men, who rush so boldly forward in pursuit of wealth, already enjoyed a comfortable living in their own part of the country. They take their wives with them and make them share the countless dangers and hardships that always accompany the start of these expeditions. I have often met young women, even on the edge of the wilderness, who had been raised amid all the comforts of the large towns of New England and had gone, almost without any intermediate stage, from their parents’ wealthy home to a comfortless hovel in a forest. Fever, solitude and a tedious life had not broken the springs of their courage. Their features were worn and faded, but their looks were firm; they seemed at once sad and resolute. I do not doubt that these young American women had stored up, in the education of their early years, the inward strength they showed in these circumstances. In the United States, then, the girl’s early training can still be traced in the married woman. Her role has changed and her habits are different, but her character is the same.
